title: 'Little Black Boy' and Ethel Waters' recording
summary: Whiting wrote a sermon-like lyric for Johnson's title 'Little Black Boy'; only Ethel Waters recorded it and Johnson disliked her interpretation.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Oh, you've stirred up your head enough. You really collaborated with great people, and great people collaborated with you. That's marvelous.

Well, one of the things George Whiting wrote -- I said to him, this is a good thing, I'd say, "Hey, George, I've got a title and I don't know whether you would like it or not, but I'll tell it to you if you want to hear it" and he'd say, "Of course I want to hear it." I said "Little Black Boy," and he turned away from me -- completely away from me, we were looking at each other, and he turned his back completely away from me, and I didn't say a word and he turned back and he said, "Get me a tune, and I'll be ready". And we wrote, "Little Black Boy" later when I got a beautiful tune. He was ready, all right, because that is one of the loveliest lyrics you'd ever want to see.
He preached a sermon in that lyric, he practically preached a sermon in that lyric.
Do you have that on record?
Yes. I have only one person made it -- Ethel Waters.
Oh! All right, that's another treasure.
She sang it -- she was the only
one, and I didn't like her interpreting it -- da, da, da, you remember that? She interpreted that in that lyric, and I didn't think it was necessary to interpret anything.
Right, it was sort of contrived at that point.
Yes. But that was the way she felt it should be done -- but I think I went and got that crushed out, I think. That part. I'm pretty sure I got it crushed out, and sewed it back together again.

Aha, that's the way to do it, that's the way to do it. JC, being with you is like a little heaven for me, because you share so many lovely moments, and I'll be back again next week, and today we'll say so long for January 30th, 1979, and hello, February, coming up.
